questions.q: What does PostgreSQL streaming replication actually stream from primary to standby?
options: WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records, as they're generated
A nightly full backup file
Individual SQL statements re-parsed on the standby
A compressed snapshot of the entire data directory, once per hour
questions.explain: Streaming replication ships WAL records continuously as they're generated, rather than waiting for them to be archived to a file.

questions.q: Which two processes carry out the streaming itself, per this lesson?
options: A WAL sender process on the primary and a WAL receiver process on the standby
pg_dump on the primary and pg_restore on the standby
The autovacuum daemon on both servers
pg_basebackup running continuously in the background
questions.explain: The WAL sender on the primary streams WAL records; the WAL receiver on the standby writes and replays them.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between physical and logical replication?
options: Physical replication ships WAL and produces a byte-for-byte full-cluster copy; logical replication replicates selectively at the row/table level
Physical replication is selective by table; logical replication always copies the entire cluster
They are two names for exactly the same mechanism
Logical replication cannot be used for high availability, so it doesn't exist in PostgreSQL
questions.explain: Physical replication is WAL-based and copies everything; logical replication, covered in Lesson 82, uses publish/subscribe to replicate specific tables.

questions.q: Roughly how much lag should you expect on a healthy physical streaming standby, per this lesson?
options: Typically well under a second, though not literally zero and worth monitoring
Always exactly zero, with no possible lag
Around 24 hours, since replication is batch-based
Lag is undefined and impossible to reason about
questions.explain: Because replay happens as WAL records arrive, near-real-time in practice means sub-second lag on a healthy standby, not instantaneous replication.

questions.q: Does streaming replication by itself automate failover if the primary goes down?
options: No — it keeps a current copy of the data ready, but promotion and client redirection are separate concerns
Yes — the standby automatically becomes the new primary and clients reconnect instantly
Yes, but only for logical replication, never for physical replication
Failover is automatic but always takes exactly 24 hours
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that streaming replication keeps a standby current but does not itself automate promotion or failover; that's handled by separate tooling.
